        ;; Kill diff buffers that were created
        (dolist (buf (buffer-list))
          (when (string-match-p "^\\*Diff\\*" (buffer-name buf))
            (kill-buffer buf)))
        ;; Call the original exit function, skipping modified buffer checks
        (let ((buffers-save-without-query

                                     (and (buffer-file-name buf)

                                   (buffer-list)))))

;; Override the default keybinding and menu item
(global-set-key (kbd "C-x C-c") #'my/save-buffers-kill-emacs)

# Technical Requirements for CAN Interface Timing Requirement (ISO 26262)

## Functional Requirement
> *"CAN Interface shall need less than 50 ms to send out a signal after receiving it from a software module."*

---

## Technical Requirements Derived for ISO 26262 Compliance

### 1. **Timing & Performance Requirements**

| ID | Technical Requirement |
|----|----------------------|
| TR-01 | The CAN driver shall transmit a CAN frame within **≤ 50 ms** from the timestamp of software module signal handover |
| TR-02 | The worst-case end-to-end latency (software handover → CAN bus transmission) shall be **≤ 50 ms** under all operating conditions (temperature, voltage, load) |
| TR-03 | The CAN transmission scheduling shall guarantee **deterministic timing** with a maximum jitter of **[X ms]** (to be derived from system budget) |
| TR-04 | CAN bus load shall be maintained **≤ 80%** to ensure transmission within the timing budget |
| TR-05 | Task/interrupt period for CAN transmission handler shall be defined to meet the 50 ms deadline (e.g., periodic task ≤ **10 ms** cycle) |

---

### 2. **Hardware Interface Requirements**

| ID | Technical Requirement |
|----|----------------------|
| TR-06 | The CAN controller hardware shall support a **minimum baud rate** sufficient to transmit required frames within timing budget (e.g., ≥ 500 kbps for CAN 2.0, ≥ 2 Mbps for CAN FD) |
| TR-07 | CAN transceiver propagation delay shall be **≤ [X µs]** (typically < 250 µs per ISO 11898) |
| TR-08 | The microcontroller CAN peripheral interrupt latency shall be **≤ [X µs]** and documented |
| TR-09 | Hardware message buffer/mailbox allocation shall ensure **no buffer overflow** causing transmission delay > 50 ms |

---

### 3. **Software Architecture Requirements**

| ID | Technical Requirement |
|----|----------------------|
| TR-10 | The CAN Interface software module shall be implemented as an **AUTOSAR ComStack** compliant layer (COM → PDU Router → CanIf → CAN Driver) |
| TR-11 | Each software layer transition latency shall be **budgeted and documented** (timing budget allocation) |
| TR-12 | The CAN transmission task shall be assigned a **sufficient priority** in the RTOS/OS to meet the 50 ms deadline |
| TR-13 | **Interrupt-driven** or **event-triggered** transmission shall be used if polling cannot guarantee 50 ms deadline |
| TR-14 | Transmit queue depth shall be sized to prevent blocking that could cause deadline violation |

---

### 4. **Safety Requirements (ISO 26262 Specific)**

| ID | Technical Requirement | ASIL |
|----|----------------------|------|
| TR-15 | A **deadline monitoring mechanism** shall detect violation of the 50 ms transmission window and report a safety-relevant error | Dependent on ASIL level |
| TR-16 | A **watchdog or timeout** shall be implemented to detect CAN transmission failure within **[X ms]** (≤ 50 ms) | ASIL B/C/D |
| TR-17 | **E2E protection** (e.g., AUTOSAR E2E Profile) shall be applied if the signal is safety-relevant per ISO 26262-6 | ASIL B+ |
| TR-18 | Timing violation shall trigger a **safe state transition** or fault reaction as defined in the Safety Concept | ASIL dependent |
| TR-19 | The 50 ms requirement shall be verified under **worst-case CPU load** conditions (e.g., ≥ 90% load scenario) | All ASIL |
| TR-20 | **Bus-off recovery time** shall not cause a timing violation exceeding 50 ms without triggering a fault notification | ASIL B+ |

---

### 5. **Fault Detection & Diagnostic Requirements**

| ID | Technical Requirement |
|----|----------------------|
| TR-21 | The CAN driver shall detect and report **transmission errors** (ACK error, bit error, form error) within **[X ms]** |
| TR-22 | A **DTC (Diagnostic Trouble Code)** shall be stored if the 50 ms deadline is missed more than **[N] consecutive times** |
| TR-23 | The system shall distinguish between **transient** and **permanent** timing violations for fault management |
| TR-24 | **TxConfirmation callback** shall be used to verify successful transmission and measure actual latency |

---

### 6. **Verification & Validation Requirements**

| ID | Technical Requirement |
|----|----------------------|
| TR-25 | The 50 ms latency shall be **measurable via hardware tracing** (e.g., oscilloscope trigger, logic analyzer on CAN bus) |
| TR-26 | Timing requirement shall be verified by **worst-case execution time (WCET) analysis** at unit and integration level |
| TR-27 | **Stress testing** shall be performed at maximum bus load (80%) to verify the 50 ms requirement holds |
| TR-28 | Timing compliance shall be demonstrated in **Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL)** test environment |
| TR-29 | Test cases shall cover **boundary conditions**: exactly 50 ms, 49 ms, and 51 ms to verify monitoring behavior |

---

### 7. **Configuration & Calibration Requirements**

| ID | Technical Requirement |
|----|----------------------|
| TR-30 | The 50 ms deadline value shall be **configurable as a parameter** (not hardcoded) to allow system-level adjustment |
| TR-31 | CAN baud rate, message priority, and task period shall be **documented in the system configuration file** |

---

## Timing Budget Breakdown Example

```
Software Module Signal Handover
         │
         ▼
[COM Layer]          ~1-2 ms  (task period)
         │
         ▼
[PDU Router]         ~0.1 ms
         │
         ▼
[CanIf Layer]        ~0.1 ms
         │
         ▼
[CAN Driver]         ~1-2 ms  (task period / interrupt)
         │
         ▼
[CAN Controller HW]  ~µs range
         │
         ▼
[CAN Transceiver]    <250 µs
         │
         ▼
CAN Bus Signal
─────────────────────────────
Total Budget:        ≤ 50 ms
Safety Margin:       ~45 ms used → 5 ms margin recommended
```

---

## Key ISO 26262 References

| Standard Part | Relevance |
|---------------|-----------|
| **ISO 26262-4** | System-level technical safety requirements |
| **ISO 26262-6** | Software safety requirements (timing, E2E) |
| **ISO 26262-8** | Safety-related interfaces, E2E communication |
| **ISO 26262-9** | ASIL decomposition if applicable |
| **AUTOSAR E2E** | End-to-end protection for signal integrity |

---

> ⚠️ **Note:** The actual ASIL level assignment depends on the HARA (Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment). The 50 ms value should be traceable back to a **safety goal** and verified through **Fault Tree Analysis (FTA)** or **FMEA** at system level.

# Technical Requirements for ISO 26262

## Functional Requirement
**FR-HMI-001:** HMI shall be able to disable buttons on center display if the needed vehicle condition for that function is not given.

---

## Technical Requirements

---

### TR-HMI-001-01 | Button State Evaluation
**The HMI software shall evaluate the enabling conditions for each button on the center display upon every display refresh cycle or upon any change in vehicle state signals, whichever occurs first.**

- **Rationale:** Ensures button states are always synchronized with current vehicle conditions without unnecessary delay.
- **Verification Method:** Test
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-02 | Button Disable Response Time
**The HMI software shall disable a button on the center display within ≤ 200 ms after the corresponding vehicle condition transitions to a "not fulfilled" state.**

- **Rationale:** Ensures the driver/user cannot interact with a function that is no longer available, reducing risk of unintended activation.
- **Verification Method:** Test
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-03 | Button Enable Response Time
**The HMI software shall re-enable a button on the center display within ≤ 200 ms after all corresponding vehicle enabling conditions transition to a "fulfilled" state.**

- **Rationale:** Ensures timely availability of functions once conditions are met.
- **Verification Method:** Test
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-04 | Disable State Visual Indication
**When a button is disabled, the HMI shall render the button in a visually distinct "grayed-out" or inactive state, clearly differentiable from the enabled state, in accordance with the HMI Style Guide [REF-STYLE-GUIDE-001].**

- **Rationale:** Provides clear feedback to the user that the function is not available.
- **Verification Method:** Inspection / Test
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-05 | Disabled Button Input Rejection
**The HMI software shall not process or forward any user input event (touch, press, swipe) triggered on a disabled button to the corresponding application or vehicle function.**

- **Rationale:** Prevents unintended function activation when vehicle preconditions are not satisfied.
- **Verification Method:** Test
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-06 | Vehicle Condition Signal Interface
**The HMI software shall receive vehicle condition signals required for button enabling logic via a defined interface (e.g., CAN, automotive Ethernet, internal IPC) as specified in the Signal Database [REF-SDB-001], with a maximum signal reception timeout of ≤ 100 ms.**

- **Rationale:** Defines the interface contract for receiving vehicle state data needed to evaluate enabling conditions.
- **Verification Method:** Test / Review
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-07 | Signal Timeout Handling – Default to Disabled
**If a vehicle condition signal required for a button's enabling logic is not received within the defined timeout period (≤ 100 ms), the HMI shall treat the condition as "not fulfilled" and disable the corresponding button.**

- **Rationale:** Fail-safe behavior ensures that missing or delayed signals do not result in an erroneously enabled button.
- **Verification Method:** Test
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-08 | Signal Plausibility Check
**The HMI software shall perform a plausibility check on received vehicle condition signals (range check, valid value check) before using them to determine button state. Signals failing plausibility checks shall be treated as "not fulfilled."**

- **Rationale:** Prevents corrupt or out-of-range signal values from incorrectly enabling buttons.
- **Verification Method:** Test
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-09 | Per-Button Condition Configuration
**The enabling conditions for each button shall be individually configurable via a dedicated configuration artifact (e.g., XML, JSON configuration table) without requiring changes to HMI core software logic.**

- **Rationale:** Ensures scalability and maintainability when new functions or condition changes are introduced across vehicle variants.
- **Verification Method:** Inspection / Review
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-10 | Multiple Condition Support (AND/OR Logic)
**The HMI software shall support evaluation of multiple vehicle conditions per button using configurable logical operators (AND, OR, or combination thereof) as defined in the button configuration artifact.**

- **Rationale:** Reflects real-world scenarios where button availability depends on multiple simultaneous or alternative vehicle states.
- **Verification Method:** Test
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-11 | Feedback Message for Disabled Button Interaction**
**When a user attempts to interact with a disabled button, the HMI shall optionally display a contextual message or tooltip indicating the reason for unavailability, as specified in the button configuration artifact.**

- **Rationale:** Improves user experience by informing the user what condition must be met to enable the function.
- **Verification Method:** Test
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-12 | Logging of Button State Transitions
**The HMI software shall log every button state transition (enabled → disabled, disabled → enabled) including a timestamp, button identifier, and triggering signal/condition, to the system diagnostic log.**

- **Rationale:** Supports traceability, debugging, and post-event analysis in accordance with ISO 26262 diagnostic requirements.
- **Verification Method:** Test
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-13 | Safe State During HMI Software Fault
**In the event of an HMI software fault that prevents evaluation of vehicle conditions, the HMI shall default all affected buttons to the disabled state.**

- **Rationale:** Fail-safe behavior ensures that a software error cannot result in a button being erroneously available.
- **Verification Method:** Test
- **ASIL:** QM

---

### TR-HMI-001-14 | Consistency Across Display Instances
**If the same button or function is presented on multiple display pages or in multiple widgets simultaneously, all instances shall reflect the same enabled/disabled state at all times.**

- **Rationale:** Prevents inconsistency that could mislead the user or allow activation through an alternative UI path.
- **Verification Method:** Test
- **ASIL:** QM

# How to Choose a Sport Watch

## Key Factors to Consider

### 1. **Define Your Sport/Activity**
- Running → GPS accuracy, pace tracking
- Swimming → Water resistance, stroke count
- Cycling → Power meter compatibility, cadence
- Hiking → Altimeter, compass, topographic maps
- Cross-training → Multi-sport modes

---

### 2. **Essential Features**
| Feature | Why It Matters |
|--------|---------------|
| **GPS** | Tracks routes and distance accurately |
| **Heart Rate Monitor** | Monitors training intensity |
| **Battery Life** | Longer for endurance activities |
| **Water Resistance** | Important for swimmers/triathletes |
| **Durability** | Withstands impact and elements |

---

### 3. **Battery Life**
- Casual use: 1-2 days may be fine
- Endurance sports: Look for **20+ hours** GPS mode
- Ultramarathons/expeditions: Consider solar charging

---

### 4. **Comfort & Fit**
- Lightweight for running
- Secure strap for high-movement sports
- Comfortable for 24/7 wear

---

### 5. **Budget Ranges**
- **Budget ($50–150):** Basic GPS, Fitbit, Amazfit
- **Mid-range ($150–400):** Garmin Forerunner, Polar
- **Premium ($400+):** Garmin Fenix, Apple Watch Ultra, COROS

---

### 6. **Smart Features (Optional)**
- Notifications
- Music storage
- Contactless payments
- Recovery/sleep tracking

---

## Quick Recommendations by Sport
- 🏃 **Runners** → Garmin Forerunner series
- 🏊 **Swimmers** → Garmin Swim or Apple Watch
- 🧗 **Outdoor/Hiking** → Garmin Fenix, Suunto
- 🚴 **Cyclists** → Wahoo, Garmin Edge (or wrist GPS)

---

**Tip:** Prioritize the features you'll *actually use* rather than buying the most advanced model.

# **"New Horizons: Welcome to the New Year"**

## PRE-EVENT LOGISTICS

### Technical Requirements
- **On-site:** Main hall with projector/large screen, cameras (minimum 2: one wide-angle for the room, one mobile for the tour), microphones for facilitators and participants, stable Wi-Fi
- **Online platform:** Zoom/Teams with breakout room capability, polling tools (Mentimeter/Slido), chat moderation
- **Materials sent to online participants 3–5 days in advance:** Workshop supply kits, printed reflection sheets, a campus map PDF for the virtual tour segment

### Roles
- **Host/MC** — leads the overall event (on-site)
- **Online Co-Host** — monitors chat, manages breakout rooms, voices online participants' questions (remote)
- **Camera Operator** — handles the mobile camera during the tour (on-site)
- **Workshop Facilitators** — one per workshop group (mixed on-site/online)
- **Technical Support** — on standby throughout

# The Tragic Flaw of Willy Loman: Self-Deception and the Destruction of the American Dream

In his foundational work on tragedy, Aristotle argues that the demise of a tragic figure "is brought about not by vice or depravity, but by some error or frailty," commonly referred to as a tragic flaw. Arthur Miller's *Death of a Salesman* presents Willy Loman as a complex and deeply flawed protagonist whose downfall raises an essential question: does Willy possess a tragic flaw in the classical Aristotelian sense, or is he simply a victim of a corrupt and unforgiving society? While some may argue that Willy is merely a casualty of the American Dream's false promises, Willy Loman does indeed possess a tragic flaw — his relentless and willful self-deception — and it is this inability to confront reality that systematically destroys his relationships, his career, his family, and ultimately his life, suggesting that Miller's broader theme is a devastating critique of a culture that manufactures illusion as a substitute for truth.

## Body Paragraph 1: Willy's Self-Deception as His Tragic Flaw

From the very opening of the play, Miller establishes Willy Loman as a man fundamentally disconnected from reality. Willy's tragic flaw is not laziness, cruelty, or immorality in the traditional sense — it is his compulsive need to believe in a version of himself and his life that simply does not exist. He has spent decades constructing an elaborate fantasy in which he is well-liked, successful, and on the verge of greatness, despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary. This self-deception is not merely an occasional lapse in judgment; it is the lens through which Willy filters every experience, every relationship, and every failure. When Linda attempts to ground him in the reality of their financial situation, noting the mounting bills and the modest nature of their income, Willy refuses to accept it, insisting instead on projecting an image of prosperity. His tragic flaw, therefore, is the active, persistent, and ultimately fatal choice to live inside a lie rather than confront the truth. This flaw aligns with Aristotle's definition because it is not pure evil that destroys Willy — it is a deeply human error, a frailty born out of pride, insecurity, and a desperate need for validation.

## Body Paragraph 2: Self-Deception and Willy's Relationship with Biff

Perhaps nowhere is Willy's self-deception more destructive than in his relationship with his son Biff. Willy has projected onto Biff all of his own unfulfilled ambitions, convincing himself that Biff is destined for greatness simply because he is well-liked and athletic. Willy raises Biff on a foundation of hollow praise and warped values, teaching him that personality and charm matter more than hard work and integrity. This becomes tragically apparent when Biff confronts Willy near the end of the play, desperate for his father to see him — and himself — clearly. Biff cries out, "I am not a leader of men, Willy, and neither are you. You were never anything but a hard-working drummer who landed in the ash can like all the rest of them!" (Miller 132). This moment is one of the most powerful in the play because Biff is demanding truth in a household that has been built entirely on lies. Yet even in this devastating confrontation, Willy cannot fully absorb what his son is telling him. His self-deception has robbed him of the ability to engage honestly with the people he loves most. Rather than bringing father and son together, Willy's flaw has created an unbridgeable chasm between them, one that has cost Biff years of confusion and aimlessness and has cost Willy the genuine connection he so desperately craved.

## Body Paragraph 3: The Illusion of the American Dream and Willy's Professional Delusion

Willy's self-deception extends beyond his family and into his professional life, where it is equally ruinous. Throughout the play, Willy clings to a mythologized version of success rooted in the American Dream — the belief that charm, likability, and an impressive appearance are sufficient to achieve prosperity. He idolizes figures like Dave Singleman, a salesman who supposedly died "the death of a salesman" — respected, remembered, and mourned by buyers and sellers across the country. Willy tells Howard, "When he died, hundreds of salesman and buyers were at his funeral" (Miller 81). For Willy, this image of Singleman represents the pinnacle of the salesman's life, a life built not on product or skill but on personality and personal connection. What Willy refuses to acknowledge, however, is that this dream is outdated, perhaps even fictitious, and that the business world has long since moved on. Howard Wagner, Willy's young boss, does not care about Willy's decades of service or his personal relationship with Howard's father. He fires Willy with cold indifference, and in doing so, shatters the illusion that likability is a sufficient currency in the American marketplace. Willy's refusal to update his understanding of success — his insistence on the fantasy over the reality — leaves him professionally obsolete and emotionally devastated, entirely unprepared for the brutal pragmatism of modern capitalism.

## Body Paragraph 4: Self-Deception and the Path to Suicide

Willy's self-deception ultimately leads him to the most tragic and irreversible decision of his life: suicide. By the end of the play, Willy has constructed one final delusion — that his death will be a heroic, meaningful act that will provide Biff with the insurance money needed to launch a successful business venture. In his final moments, Willy is not broken and defeated; he is strangely exhilarated, convinced that he is finally on the cusp of something great. He tells the imagined ghost of Ben, "Can you imagine that magnificence with twenty thousand dollars in his pocket?" (Miller 135). This is the ultimate expression of Willy's tragic flaw. Even at the moment of his death, he is incapable of seeing clearly. He does not understand that Biff does not want the money, does not want the American Dream, and does not want his father to die. He does not understand that the insurance company may not pay out for a suicide. He does not understand that the greatest gift he could give his family is not money but honesty. Willy dies not in a moment of clarity or catharsis, but in the grip of the same delusion that has governed his entire life. His flaw does not release him at the end — it consumes him entirely.

## Conclusion: Thematic Significance

Willy Loman's tragic flaw — his willful and all-consuming self-deception — is not simply a personal failing; it is Miller's vehicle for exploring one of the most urgent themes of the twentieth century: the destructive power of the American Dream when it is pursued without honesty or self-awareness. Miller suggests that a culture which prizes image over substance, appearance over reality, and success over integrity will inevitably produce men like Willy Loman — men who are so thoroughly seduced by an illusion that they cannot survive contact with the truth. As Biff says in the Requiem, "He had the wrong dreams. All, all wrong" (Miller 138). Willy's tragedy is not simply that he failed, but that he never truly tried to succeed at anything real. His flaw leads to his demise, and his demise illuminates the hollow center of the American Dream itself — the terrifying possibility that the promises a society makes to its people can themselves become instruments of destruction. In this way, Willy Loman stands as one of literature's most enduring tragic figures, not because he is exceptional, but because he is heartbreakingly ordinary.

## Atributo `mustUnderstand` de SOAP

El atributo **`mustUnderstand`** de SOAP se usa para indicar si la entrada del header es **obligatoria u opcional** por el receptor para ser procesada.

### Funcionamiento:

| Valor | Significado |
|-------|-------------|
| `mustUnderstand="1"` (o `true`) | El receptor **debe** procesar el header; si no puede, debe generar un fault |
| `mustUnderstand="0"` (o `false`) | El procesamiento del header es **opcional** |

### Ejemplo:

```xml
<soap:Envelope xmlns:soap="http://www.w3.org/2003/05/soap-envelope">
  <soap:Header>
    <auth:Authentication 
      xmlns:auth="http://ejemplo.com/auth"
      soap:mustUnderstand="1">
        <auth:token>abc123</auth:token>
    </auth:Authentication>
  </soap:Header>
  <soap:Body>
    ...
  </soap:Body>
</soap:Envelope>
```

> Si el receptor **no reconoce** o **no puede procesar** un header con `mustUnderstand="1"`, está obligado a retornar un error **SOAP Fault**.

## Ошибка в SQL запросе

`None` — это значение из **Python**, а не SQL. В SQL нужно использовать `NULL`.

---

### ❌ Неправильно:
```sql
SELECT * FROM public.tasks
WHERE tasks.url not None
```

### ✅ Правильно:
```sql
SELECT * FROM public.tasks
WHERE tasks.url IS NOT NULL
```

---

## Разница между Python и SQL:

| | Python | SQL |
|---|---|---|
| Пустое значение | `None` | `NULL` |
| Проверка на пустоту | `!= None` или `is not None` | `IS NOT NULL` |
| Проверка на наличие | `== None` или `is None` | `IS NULL` |

---

### ⚠️ Важно:
В SQL нельзя использовать `= NULL` или `!= NULL` — только **`IS NULL`** и **`IS NOT NULL`**, потому что `NULL` означает **отсутствие значения** и не может быть сравнено обычными операторами.

# The Fractured Self: Subjectivity and Objectivity in Birdman's Cinematic Vision

## Exploring Riggan Thomson's Interior and Exterior World Through the Camera

Alejandro González Iñárritu's *Birdman or (The Unexpected Virtue of Ignorance)* (2014) is a film fundamentally preoccupied with the dissolution of boundaries — between success and failure, relevance and obsolescence, sanity and delusion. At its narrative and philosophical center stands Riggan Thomson, a faded Hollywood superhero actor attempting to resurrect his artistic credibility through a Broadway production of Raymond Carver's *What We Talk About When We Talk About Love*. What makes the film cinematically extraordinary is the way Emmanuel Lubezki's camera refuses to cleanly separate Riggan's subjective interior experience from the objective external world he inhabits. This deliberate blending creates a visual and psychological space where fantasy bleeds into reality, where backstage vulnerability confronts onstage performance, and where the audience is never entirely certain what is real and what is the desperate invention of a disintegrating mind. The camera, in this sense, becomes the most honest and destabilizing narrator of Riggan's profound internal and external conflicts.

## The Illusion of the Continuous Take

The film's most immediately striking formal choice is its apparent construction as a single, uninterrupted take — a seamless flow of movement through the bowels of the St. James Theatre and onto the streets of New York City. This technique is not merely a stylistic flourish; it is a profound statement about Riggan's psychological condition. Traditional editing creates cognitive pauses, moments where an audience can breathe, reorient, and distinguish between different emotional registers or narrative positions. By eliminating those cuts, Iñárritu and Lubezki eliminate the visual grammar that would normally separate the subjective from the objective. Riggan's paranoid inner monologue, his telekinetic fantasies, his hallucinatory conversations with the Birdman persona — these exist within the same unbroken visual flow as conversations with his daughter Sam, his ex-wife Sylvia, and his collaborators. The continuous camera refuses to grant the audience the privilege of clean categorization. Reality and delusion share the same cinematic breath.

## The Birdman Voice and the Camera's Complicity

The Birdman persona — that deep, rasping, mocking internal voice that narrates Riggan's self-doubt and grandiosity simultaneously — represents the most explicit articulation of his subjective reality. When Riggan exercises telekinetic powers in his dressing room, levitating objects and shattering mirrors, the camera observes these moments with the same steady, unblinking attention it gives to objectively verifiable scenes. There is no cinematic signal — no distorted lens, no dramatic shift in lighting — that definitively marks these moments as fantasy. The camera is complicit in Riggan's delusion. It validates his subjective experience by refusing to visually pathologize it. This creates a deeply unsettling viewing experience because the audience must inhabit Riggan's perspective without the safety of knowing where truth ends and invention begins. The famous sequence where Riggan flies above the Manhattan skyline, soaring between skyscrapers in his Birdman costume, is presented with such visual confidence and kinetic joy that it functions simultaneously as obvious fantasy and as a manifestation of Riggan's most sincere emotional truth — his desperate longing for transcendence, for a version of himself that cannot be wounded by critics, abandoned by audiences, or humiliated by superior talent.

## Backstage and Onstage: The Collapse of Authentic and Performed Identity

The theatrical setting of *Birdman* allows the film to explore with extraordinary richness the tension between the performed self and the authentic self — or, more disturbingly, the question of whether any authentic self exists at all. The camera tracks Riggan through the narrow, claustrophobic corridors of the St. James Theatre with an almost predatory intimacy. Backstage, stripped of costume and spotlight, Riggan is at his most exposed — arguing with his daughter, pleading with his producer, confronting his own mediocrity. These backstage spaces are shot with a restless, probing energy, the camera pressing close to Riggan's face, catching the sweat and desperation that his public persona labors to conceal. The theatre's backstage becomes an objective space that nevertheless feels deeply subjective — a psychological landscape that mirrors Riggan's inner fragmentation, its labyrinthine corridors suggesting a self that cannot find its own center.

Onstage, however, something paradoxical occurs. The moment Riggan steps into the spotlight, the camera opens up, the space expands, and there is a strange visual coherence to the performance. Yet the film complicates this by staging the most emotionally authentic moments of Riggan's journey as theatrical performances. When Riggan loads the prop gun with a real bullet for the final performance, the distinction between onstage drama and offstage crisis collapses entirely. The camera holds this moment with devastating stillness. The theatrical act of shooting himself in the face becomes simultaneously a performance for an audience, a suicide attempt, and, in its aftermath, a bizarre act of artistic self-creation. The objective reality — a man shoots himself — and the subjective reality — a man transcends himself — are rendered cinematically inseparable.

## The Street as Psychological Landscape

Beyond the theatre, the film's excursion onto the streets of New York City further illustrates the camera's blending of interior and exterior conflict. The sequence in which Riggan, locked out of the theatre in his underwear, must traverse Times Square to re-enter through the front door is both objectively humiliating and subjectively liberating. The camera captures the crowd's mockery with documentary-like clarity while simultaneously tracking Riggan's almost ecstatic surrender to public humiliation. The external world becomes a mirror for his internal state, the chaos of Times Square reflecting the chaos within.

## Conclusion

*Birdman* ultimately uses its camera not as a passive recorder of events but as a participant in Riggan Thomson's psychological reality. By blending subjective and objective registers within a continuous, unbroken visual flow, the film refuses to adjudicate between sanity and madness, performance and authenticity, fantasy and truth. The camera explores Riggan's internal conflicts — his terror of irrelevance, his hunger for genuine artistic expression — and his external conflicts — his fractured relationships, his professional humiliations — as fundamentally indivisible. In doing so, *Birdman* suggests something deeply uncomfortable: that for an actor, and perhaps for all of us, the self is nothing more and nothing less than the performance we sustain when no one is supposed to be watching.

## Step 4: Basic Usage with LangChain

### Using llama-cpp-python (GGUF)

```python
from langchain.llms import LlamaCpp
from langchain.prompts import PromptTemplate
from langchain.chains import LLMChain

# Load Vicuna model
llm = LlamaCpp(
    model_path="./models/vicuna-7b-v1.5.Q4_K_M.gguf",
    temperature=0.7,
    max_tokens=512,
    n_ctx=4096,        # context window
    n_gpu_layers=40,   # set to 0 for CPU only
    verbose=True
)

# Create prompt template (Vicuna format)
template = """A chat between a curious user and an assistant.
USER: {question}
ASSISTANT:"""

prompt = PromptTemplate(
    template=template,
    input_variables=["question"]
)

# Create chain
chain = LLMChain(prompt=prompt, llm=llm)

# Run
response = chain.run("What is the capital of France?")
print(response)
```

---

### Using Transformers

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM, pipeline
from langchain.llms import HuggingFacePipeline
from langchain.prompts import PromptTemplate
from langchain.chains import LLMChain
import torch

model_id = "lmsys/vicuna-7b-v1.5"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    torch_dtype=torch.float16,
    device_map="auto"
)

# Create pipeline
pipe = pipeline(
    "text-generation",
    model=model,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    max_new_tokens=512,
    temperature=0.7,
    device_map="auto"
)

# Wrap with LangChain
llm = HuggingFacePipeline(pipeline=pipe)

# Create chain
template = """USER: {question}
ASSISTANT:"""

prompt = PromptTemplate(template=template, input_variables=["question"])
chain = LLMChain(prompt=prompt, llm=llm)

response = chain.run("Explain quantum computing")
print(response)
```

---

## Step 5: Advanced - RAG with Vicuna + LangChain

```python
from langchain.llms import LlamaCpp
from langchain.embeddings import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
from langchain.vectorstores import FAISS
from langchain.chains import RetrievalQA
from langchain.document_loaders import TextLoader
from langchain.text_splitter import CharacterTextSplitter

# Load documents
loader = TextLoader("your_document.txt")
documents = loader.load()

# Split text
text_splitter = CharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=500, chunk_overlap=50)
texts = text_splitter.split_documents(documents)

# Create embeddings & vector store
embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
vectorstore = FAISS.from_documents(texts, embeddings)

# Load Vicuna
llm = LlamaCpp(
    model_path="./models/vicuna-7b-v1.5.Q4_K_M.gguf",
    n_gpu_layers=40,
    n_ctx=4096,
    temperature=0.1
)

# Create RAG chain
qa_chain = RetrievalQA.from_chain_type(
    llm=llm,
    retriever=vectorstore.as_retriever(),
    return_source_documents=True
)

result = qa_chain("Your question here?")
print(result["result"])
```

---

### Challenges
- Most Vicuna models start at **7B parameters**

- The GTX 750 will likely need to run mostly on **CPU/RAM**

---

### Possible Options

**Vicuna-7B with heavy quantization (GGUF format)**
- Run with **llama.cpp**
- Use **Q2_K or Q3_K** quantization
- Offload most/all layers to CPU
- Will be **very slow** but technically possible

**Recommendations for your hardware:**
- Use **llama.cpp** with CPU inference primarily
- Your **RAM matters more** than VRAM here (need 8GB+)
- Consider **Vicuna-7B Q2_K** (~2.5GB)

---

### Tools to Try
- **LM Studio** - easy GUI, handles quantized models
- **Ollama** - simple command line
- **llama.cpp** - direct control over GPU/CPU layer splitting

---

### Realistic Expectation
Expect **very slow generation** (possibly 1-3 tokens/second) with most work done on CPU.

# NECROPOLIS NOVA
## A Post-Apocalyptic City Setting for Tabletop Roleplaying Games

---

# BACKGROUND LORE

## The Spore Plague of 2129

They called it **the Darkening**.

It began in the autumn of 2129, first reported as an aggressive fungal infection spreading through the water supply of three megacities simultaneously — too fast, too coordinated to be natural. Within eighteen months, **90% of the world's population** was dead, dying, or worse. The virus — officially designated **Mycorvax-7** by the last functioning CDC outpost before it went silent — was unlike anything ever catalogued. Part fungal, part viral, part something that biologists still argue about in hushed, frightened voices seventy years later.

Mycorvax-7 didn't just kill. It *transformed*. Those it didn't kill outright became hosts. Dark, thread-like spores colonized nervous systems, muscle tissue, and bone. Animals twisted into grotesque shapes. Humans became shambling, aggressive horrors called **the Blighted** — humanoid masses of dark fungal growth, exposed bone, and feral cunning, driven by a collective hunger that researchers believe may be directed by some form of hive intelligence no one has yet fully understood.

The city once known as **New Avalon** — a sprawling coastal megacity of ten million souls, a jewel of 22nd-century architecture, vertical farms, magnetic transit, and corporate utopian promises — became something else. Something darker. Something that barely survived.

---

## The City Today: 2199

Seventy years after the Darkening, the survivors renamed the city **Necropolis Nova** — half irony, half truth. A city of the dead that refuses to die.

Between **200,000 and 300,000 people** cling to life within its walls and towers. They are the children and grandchildren of survivors, the immune, the lucky, the brutal, and the brilliant. The city is enclosed by a massive, imperfect barrier system — a patchwork of reinforced walls, magnetized fencing, repurposed construction debris, and automated turret systems — collectively called **The Perimeter**. Beyond The Perimeter, the world belongs to the Blighted and the wild mutant hordes. Inside, humanity holds on.

But *just* holding on is not the same as thriving.

Resources are scarce. Clean water is politics. Food is power. Technology from the old world still functions in places — and is fought over savagely. Three generations of survivors have produced people who have never known anything but this city, its dangers, its factions, and its grudging, grimy beauty.

And then there are the **Touched** — humans who, through some quirk of genetics or prolonged exposure to low-level Mycorvax-7 spores, have developed abilities that defy easy explanation. Some can feel the presence of the Blighted like a cold pressure behind the eyes. Some heal faster than they should. Some hear things. Some *do* things. They are feared, revered, recruited, and hunted, depending entirely on who finds them first.

---

## A Note on the Mutants

The Blighted and other mutant creatures exist **beyond The Perimeter**. They do not — cannot, under normal circumstances — enter the city districts. The Perimeter holds. *Mostly*. There are breaches. There are sections that haven't been fully repaired since the last major incursion twelve years ago. There are smugglers who move through the outer zones and bring things back with them. There are rumors of tunnels beneath the old subway network that the Blighted have learned to navigate.

Inside Necropolis Nova, the monsters wear human faces.

---

# THE DISTRICTS OF NECROPOLIS NOVA

The city is divided into **nine distinct districts**, each with its own culture, power structure, economy, and problems. They are connected by the partially functional **Elevated Transit Network (ETN)** — a skeletal above-ground rail system that runs roughly circular lines — as well as by ground roads in varying states of repair, and by the labyrinthine network of **The Undercity** below.

---

## DISTRICT ONE: THE PINNACLE
*"Those who look down never look up."*

### Overview
The Pinnacle occupies the northeastern corner of Necropolis Nova and is built vertically — a cluster of twelve surviving skyscrapers ranging from thirty to eighty stories tall, connected by enclosed sky-bridges, pressurized transit tubes, and elegant walkways that gleam even now. From the ground, The Pinnacle looks like something out of the old world: glass still catches the light, lights still glow in windows at night, and automated cleaning drones still crawl the outer facades in a ritual of futile elegance.

Below the thirtieth floor of any building in The Pinnacle, things get complicated. Above it, The Pinnacle is the closest thing Necropolis Nova has to the world that was.

### Population & Demographics
Roughly **15,000 to 20,000 people** live in The Pinnacle, but they consume a wildly disproportionate share of the city's resources. The population is divided sharply between the **Upper Floors** (above the 30th) and the **Mid-Floors** (10th–29th). Below the 10th floor of any building, the space is given over to security operations, logistics, docking for aerial vehicles, and the servant class — the **Floor Workers** — who keep everything functioning.

The Upper Floors house the city's wealthiest and most powerful individuals: the heads of the corporate remnants that survived the Darkening, successful black market barons who laundered their fortunes into legitimacy, the most senior officers of the city's military apparatus, and a small, intensely insular intellectual class.

The Mid-Floors are home to administrators, skilled engineers, doctors, lawyers — a professional class that lives in genuine comfort relative to most of the city, but exists in constant anxiety about the distance between themselves and the floor below.

### Architecture & Atmosphere
The sky-bridges between towers are social spaces as much as transit corridors — lined with small shops, cafés running on hydroponic supplies, and art galleries displaying work that tries very hard to look like nothing bad has ever happened. There's a cultivated, aggressive normalcy to The Pinnacle that unnerves outsiders. Music plays from hidden speakers. The air is filtered. You can almost forget.

At night, The Pinnacle's lit windows cast long, warm light down into the dark city below — visible from almost every district. To most residents of Necropolis Nova, those lights mean something. For some, hope. For others, fury.

### Key Locations

**The Spire Council Chambers** — The topmost floors of the tallest building have been converted into the meeting halls of the **Spire Council**, the closest thing Necropolis Nova has to a formal governing body. Marble salvaged from old civic buildings lines the corridors. Decisions made here ripple outward to every corner of the city — sometimes immediately, sometimes in ways that take months to be felt. The Council chamber is also the most surveilled space in the city: every word spoken in the official chambers is recorded. Every word spoken in the corridors outside is *also* recorded. This is considered polite.

**The Atrium Market** — A vast, glass-roofed market space in the lobby of what was once New Avalon's premier luxury hotel. Now it functions as the high-end trading floor of the city, where everything from clean water contracts to salvage rights to human expertise is bought and sold by well-dressed people who don't raise their voices. The Atrium Market is technically neutral ground. This agreement has been tested four times. It has held four times. Barely.

**The Archive of New Avalon** — A privately maintained collection of pre-Darkening data, physical media, books, and records, housed in a climate-controlled floor of one of the mid-towers. Access is restricted and expensive. The archivist — an old woman known only as **Mme. Voss** — knows exactly what she has and exactly what it's worth.

**The Garden Floors** — Three floors of one tower have been entirely converted to an enclosed hydroponic garden of extraordinary beauty and productivity. Flowers grow here, alongside vegetables and herbs. The air tastes clean. Armed guards stand at every entrance. The Garden Floors supply fresh produce exclusively to The Pinnacle's upper residents, and the waiting list for a dinner that includes fresh food is eighteen months long.

### Atmosphere for Play
The Pinnacle is a place of *political* danger — assassination, betrayal, manipulation, and corporate intrigue. The real violence here is conducted through paperwork, whisper campaigns, and the occasional quiet disappearance. For players who enjoy intrigue, moral compromise, and the grinding machinery of power, The Pinnacle rewards deep exploration. The smiling faces here are the most dangerous in the city.

### Story Seeds
- A mid-floor administrator has discovered an irregularity in the water distribution records that suggests someone in the Upper Floors has been quietly redirecting supply for months. She needs someone discreet. She's already been warned once.
- A Floor Worker has smuggled something up from The Undercity — something that shouldn't exist. She's trying to sell it before it sells her.
- A seat on the Spire Council has just opened following the sudden illness of one of its senior members. Three factions are maneuvering simultaneously to fill it. Each believes the others don't know what they're doing. None of them are correct.

---

## DISTRICT TWO: THE SHAMBLES
*"Nobody's poor here. We just haven't been paid yet."*

### Overview
If The Pinnacle is the head of Necropolis Nova, The Shambles is its stomach — vast, necessary, faintly disgusting, and absolutely impossible to live without. Spreading across the old city center's flatlands to the south and west of The Pinnacle, The Shambles is the largest residential district by area and population, housing somewhere between **80,000 and 100,000 people** in conditions that range from cramped-but-dignified to genuinely squalid.

The Shambles was already the working-class district of New Avalon before the Darkening. Post-apocalypse, it simply became more so, as survivors flooded in from other areas of the city and the available housing stock was divided, subdivided, and divided again. Buildings designed for four families house forty. Corridors have become permanent markets. Rooftops are covered in improvised greenhouse structures, wind turbines, and water collectors.

### Population & Demographics
The population of The Shambles is the most diverse in the city — a patchwork of every background, profession, and circumstance that Necropolis Nova contains. Former corporate workers live next to scrap dealers live next to ex-soldiers live next to children who have never known anything else. The common denominator is a certain grim pragmatism: life in The Shambles is a series of small problems to be solved before they become large ones.

There's a strong sense of community here — born less from warmth than from necessity. People watch out for each other because not watching out for each other is how you end up dead.

### Architecture & Atmosphere
The Shambles has the look of a city that was being repaired constantly but never quite finished. Buildings are a patchwork of original structure and survival-era additions — concrete blocks shored up with salvaged steel, windows covered in plastic sheeting or boarded entirely, external staircases bolted onto facades at odd angles. The streets are narrow and permanently busy, the air smells of cooking, machine oil, damp concrete, and occasionally something less identifiable.

Color is everywhere. Three generations of people with no access to entertainment industry have become their own — murals cover entire building faces, handmade signs advertise services in five languages, and the informal street shrines to the dead (a Shambles tradition) are elaborate, bright, and constantly refreshed.

At night, The Shambles lights up with improvised lighting — salvaged neon, repurposed construction lights, strings of old LEDs — and the street market economy shifts gear toward things that don't get discussed in daylight.

### Key Locations

**The Long Market** — A market that began in a single street and expanded over seventy years until it now occupies a connected network of twelve streets, three plazas, two building lobbies, and a section of elevated walkway. The Long Market is where you can find almost anything in Necropolis Nova: legitimate goods, salvage, information, contraband, services of all kinds. It is organized by a system so complex and informal that only people who grew up in it can navigate it effectively. There is supposedly a master directory kept by the **Market Guild** — a loose association of senior vendors — but outsiders have never been allowed to see it.

**The Shambles Cisterns** — The water infrastructure beneath The Shambles is one of the most important and contested pieces of technology in the city. The old municipal water system was partially restored in the years after the Darkening, and the underground cisterns now distribute — unevenly — water to most of the district. Control of the cistern valves is a constant source of low-level conflict, managed by a complicated system of agreements between neighborhood councils that breaks down regularly.

**The Hall of Trades** — A large former civic center building that has been converted into a combination union hall, dispute resolution court, hiring ground, and neighborhood political meeting space. The Hall of Trades has no formal authority — it has no weapons, no jail, no enforceable laws — and somehow this means people mostly respect it, because it's the only space in The Shambles where conflicts can be resolved without someone getting hurt.

**The Shrine Mile** — A long, slightly curving street where the density of street shrines became so high that new construction stopped by general agreement. Now the entire street is a permanent memorial — thousands of names, photographs, objects, and handmade markers for the dead of the Darkening and the seventy years since. Candles are always burning somewhere on the Shrine Mile. People visit in grief and in habit. Outsiders sometimes come to look and leave uncomfortable.

**The Rat Warren** — The basement levels of a cluster of connected buildings in the western Shambles have been converted into a cramped, labyrinthine residential space of extraordinary density, home to roughly 3,000 people in conditions that city administrators (in their occasional surveys) describe as "sub-optimal." The residents of the Rat Warren call it home and are intensely territorial about it. The Warren has its own economy, its own social rules, and at least two organizations operating from its depths that nobody above ground can reliably identify.

### Atmosphere for Play
The Shambles is the heart of the city's street-level life — loud, complex, warm, and dangerous in the sudden, unpredictable way of crowds and scarcity. It's the best place in Necropolis Nova to find information, lose a pursuer, or disappear into a new identity. The stories here are human-scale: hunger, loyalty, small violence, desperate hope, and the extraordinary complexity of ordinary survival.

### Story Seeds
- A series of unexplained disappearances from the Rat Warren have been brushed off as people leaving or being taken by rival gangs. But three different families have now asked the same question: where do the bodies go?
- Water pressure in the eastern Shambles has been dropping for three weeks. The official explanation is maintenance. The maintenance crews say they've been locked out of the relevant cistern section. The locks are new.
- A young artist's mural on the western wall of the Long Market has been defaced twice in a week — both times with a symbol that the older residents recognize but won't explain. The artist is seventeen and furious. The older residents are frightened.

---

## DISTRICT THREE: THE FORGE
*"We build what we can't buy and break what we can't build."*

### Overview
The Forge occupies the old industrial waterfront on the western edge of the city, where New Avalon's manufacturing district met the harbor. It is the roughest district in the city by almost any metric that doesn't involve being outside The Perimeter. It smells of metal, fire, chemical processes, and the sea. It sounds like hammering.

Roughly **25,000 to 35,000 people** live and work in The Forge, in a culture that prizes physical competence, technical skill, and a specific kind of blunt directness that outsiders mistake for hostility until they spend enough time there to understand the difference.

The Forge produces things. Weapons. Components. Vehicles. Tools. Water purification systems. It maintains the automated turret networks that keep The Perimeter functional. It repairs the ETN rail cars. Without The Forge, the city would have crumbled within a generation. The Forge knows this, and the relationship between The Forge and every other district in Necropolis Nova is essentially a slow-motion negotiation about exactly how much that knowledge is worth.

### Population & Demographics
Forge workers are a mix of engineers, metalworkers, chemists, electricians, mechanics, and laborers who've inherited skills across three generations. There's a strong apprenticeship culture — children start learning trades by the time they're eight or nine, and a fully qualified Forge craftsperson is a genuinely marketable commodity across the city.

A significant minority of the population are **Scrappers** — independent salvagers who operate in the outer zones and bring raw materials back through the Perimeter gates. Scrappers occupy a strange social position in Forge culture: admired for their skill and bravery, slightly set apart by the way extended time in the outer zones seems to *change* people.

### Architecture & Atmosphere
The Forge is a district of enormous, partly functional industrial buildings — warehouses the size of city blocks, dry-dock facilities where old harbor vessels rot beautifully or have been repurposed into residential blocks, factory floors where humans and salvaged automated systems work in complicated partnership.

The air here is genuinely difficult — a combination of industrial process output and the harbor's cold, salt-tinged wind. Fires burn in old oil drums at street level. Sparks fly from upper floors. The harbor water is dark and probably toxic and absolutely beautiful in the way of ruined industrial things.

Forge workers have developed a reputation for making their living spaces extraordinary. Where The Pinnacle has elegance through preservation, The Forge has beauty through transformation — metal sculpture on every corner, intricate mechanical clocks on public buildings, tiles made from melted glass in every color pressed into the facades of residential blocks.

### Key Locations

**The Arsenal** — The largest weapons manufacturing facility in Necropolis Nova and the most heavily guarded building in The Forge. The Arsenal produces the conventional weapons that arm the city's security forces and are sold (carefully, officially) to the other districts' defense militias. The Arsenal's director, a severe engineer named **Director Mane**, reports technically to the Spire Council but has cultivated enough independent leverage — in the form of knowing where every weapon in the city came from and where it went — to operate with significant autonomy.

**The Tideyard** — The harbor's old dry-dock facilities, now a complex residential and commercial space built within and around the hulls of enormous, long-dead cargo ships. Some of the ships have been converted into multi-story housing. Others serve as covered markets, workshop spaces, and meeting halls. The Tideyard has its own internal navigation logic that is completely incomprehensible to anyone who hasn't lived there, and residents exploit this shamelessly.

**The Scrapper's Gate** — One of the few formal entry points in The Perimeter that is regularly operational. The Scrapper's Gate opens twice a day for authorized salvage teams to exit and return. There's an inspection process, a decontamination protocol, and a barter market just inside the gate where salvagers sell their finds immediately to dealers and material handlers. The Gate has its own culture — a superstitious, cautious, pragmatic culture of people who know exactly what lives outside and have decided to go there anyway.

**The Engine Hall** — A massive former turbine facility that now serves as The Forge's primary power generation center — a hybrid system of salvaged solar collection, chemical battery banks, and two functioning micro-turbines that the engineering team treats with the reverence most people reserve for religion. The Engine Hall also serves as the unofficial political center of the district, where the **Craftworkers' Assembly** meets to make decisions about collective matters.

**The Chemical Quarter** — A cluster of smaller facilities on the southern end of The Forge that produce medicines, water purification chemicals, and other chemical necessities. The Quarter is slightly apart from the rest of the district and deliberately so — several early accidents in the post-Darkening years established an understanding that the Chemical Quarter operates under its own safety protocols and its own political culture.

### Atmosphere for Play
The Forge is a place of physical drama and technical complexity. The dangers here are real and immediate — industrial accidents, territorial disputes with real knives, the return of salvagers who've seen things, and the low, constant hum of people who work with deadly things every day and have developed a healthy respect for that fact. The stories here involve loyalty, expertise, the cost of knowledge, and the strange culture of people who chose to keep going outside.

### Story Seeds
- A Scrapper team has returned from a two-week outer-zone expedition with more materials than they left with, two members fewer than they left with, and a complete unwillingness to explain either fact.
- Three pieces of Arsenal-manufactured weaponry have been found outside The Perimeter, in areas where no authorized salvage team has been in six months. Director Mane is asking quiet questions. Somebody is going to answer whether they want to or not.
- Something in the harbor has begun moving at night. Not on the surface. Below it. The Tideyard residents are keeping their children inside after dark, and the old fishermen who still cast lines off the dock walls have stopped.

---

## DISTRICT FOUR: THE CATHEDRAL
*"All gods are local. Some are just more honest about it."*

### Overview
The Cathedral district takes its name from the massive Church of the New Ascension that dominates its skyline — a pre-Darkening structure of extraordinary architectural ambition, its towers visible from most of the city. But The Cathedral is less a religious district in any singular sense than a district that has become the city's **spiritual marketplace** — every faith, philosophy, and existential framework that survived the Darkening (and several invented after it) operates here, cheek-by-jowl, in a state of permanent, sometimes violent theological negotiation.

Roughly **20,000 to 25,000 people** call The Cathedral home, with a significantly larger number moving through it daily on spiritual, social, or more practically commercial errands.

The Cathedral is located in the northeastern residential zone, between The Pinnacle and The Shambles, occupying what was New Avalon's old civic and cultural district.

### Population & Demographics
The population of The Cathedral is genuinely mixed — believers and cynics, idealists and pragmatists, the devoted and the desperate. The spiritual institutions here provide social services as well as meaning: food programs, medical care, conflict mediation, education for children, and care for the elderly. This makes The Cathedral politically important in ways that have nothing to do with theology.

There's a significant population of **scholars and teachers** in The Cathedral — people who have dedicated themselves to understanding the Darkening, the Touched, the Blighted, or simply to preserving pre-collapse knowledge in forms that can be taught.

### Architecture & Atmosphere
The Cathedral district is the most architecturally varied in the city — old civic grandeur in the central blocks, converted commercial spaces in the mid-district, and dense residential packing at the edges. The central plaza around the great church is one of the few genuinely open public spaces in Necropolis Nova, and it functions as such: a gathering place, a market of ideas, a soapbox, a meeting ground.

The streets of The Cathedral are layered with competing iconography — the symbols of a dozen faiths and philosophies painted, carved, or otherwise marked on every available surface. There's a beautiful chaos to it. A building might display the crossed-circles of the Church of the New Ascension on one wall, the spiral mark of the **Mycorvax Covenant** on an adjacent wall (those who believe Mycorvax-7 was divine), and the black-ink hand-print of the **Secular Remembrance** movement (who believe only in honoring the dead and asking practical questions) on a third.

### Key Locations

**The Church of the New Ascension** — The great church itself is an extraordinary building — pre-Darkening architecture of soaring arches and enormous stained-glass windows, most of the glass still intact. The Church of the New Ascension is also a genuine institution: it runs the district's largest hospital, feeds several thousand people daily through its food programs, and maintains the most extensive public library in the city on its lower floors. Its current head, **Arch-Speaker Ilyena Castor**, is one of the most politically significant figures in Necropolis Nova — a woman of genuine faith and complete pragmatic ruthlessness, which she sees as entirely compatible.

**The Forum of Voices** — A large, restored civic theater that has been converted into a public debate space. Anyone can apply to speak at the Forum; sessions are scheduled weekly and cover everything from theology to water policy to accounts of what people have seen in the outer zones. The Forum is moderated by a rotating council of citizens chosen by lottery. It has no power to make decisions. It has enormous power to shape opinion.

**The Touched Sanctuary** — Tucked into a narrow block in the eastern quarter, the Sanctuary is a small institution run by a quiet order called the **Sisters and Brothers of the Changed**. They provide refuge, care, and community for Touched individuals who need somewhere safe to understand what they're becoming. The Sanctuary is discreet. Most of the city knows it exists. An uneasy consensus keeps it from being overtly targeted — partly out of respect, partly out of the uncomfortable awareness that attacking the Touched has historically produced unpredictable results.

**The Covenant Hall** — The meeting place and shrine of the Mycorvax Covenant — those who believe the Darkening was a divine act of transformation rather than a catastrophe. The Covenant Hall is hung with dark fabric and decorated with stylized spore imagery. The Covenant's theology is complex and has many internal factions, ranging from the genuinely scholarly to the genuinely terrifying.

**The Undercroft** — The basement levels of several connected Cathedral-district buildings have been excavated and expanded over seventy years into a large underground complex used primarily for the storage and quiet exchange of things that multiple factions in the district have agreed, with the diplomacy of necessity, not to publicly acknowledge. The Undercroft is not *quite* criminal. It is definitively not innocent. It is, above all, useful.

### Atmosphere for Play
The Cathedral is a district of ideas, and the danger here comes from how seriously people take them. Religious conflict, intellectual assassination, the complex and sometimes tragic lives of the Touched, the endlessly creative ways humans construct meaning after catastrophe — these are the stories of The Cathedral. It is also the district most engaged with the question of *what happened*, which means it is the district with the most theories, the most dangerous knowledge, and the most people who have looked too long at things that look back.

### Story Seeds
- A document has surfaced in the Archive of New Avalon — apparently pre-Darkening — that suggests Mycorvax-7 was not natural and not an accident. Three different Cathedral factions want it. Two of them would like whoever found it to stop breathing.
- A Touched child at the Sanctuary has begun exhibiting an ability that the Sisters and Brothers have never recorded before — and that seems to affect people around her in ways she cannot control. Arch-Speaker Castor has taken a personal interest. So has someone else.
- A philosopher at the Forum of Voices has been publicly arguing that the Blighted beyond The Perimeter retain some form of consciousness and should not be killed. He has received two death threats. He has not stopped arguing. He has, however, started asking for protection.

## DISTRICT FIVE: THE GRID
*"Information is infrastructure."*

### Overview
The Grid is the strangest district in Necropolis Nova — a cluster of tech-dense blocks in the central city where the pre-Darkening information infrastructure survived in significant, functional form. Server farms still run, cooled by dedicated power systems maintained with near-religious devotion. Fiber optic networks still connect buildings. The engineers and hackers and data workers who've made The Grid their domain have built something in the ruins of the old internet that is part library, part marketplace, part surveillance network, and part something that probably needs its own category.

**12,000 to 18,000 people** live in The Grid, but its influence on the city extends far beyond its borders. Most districts with any functioning digital infrastructure are at least partially dependent on The Grid's network — and therefore, at least partially at the Grid's mercy.

The Grid is located in the center of the city, which is partly practical and partly deeply deliberate.

### Population & Demographics
Grid residents are disproportionately young — a culture has developed here of taking in children who show aptitude with systems and technology, training them up, and integrating them into the district's complex technical-social ecosystem. The culture is intensely meritocratic in a very specific sense: social position in The Grid is determined almost entirely by what you can *do* with systems. Age, physical ability, family history — these matter very little. The ability to solve a problem that nobody else can solve matters enormously.

There's a slightly unnerving quality to Grid culture that outsiders often notice: an inclination toward seeing everything as a system, including people. Not cruelty — Grid residents can be remarkably generous — but a particular kind of abstraction that makes some visitors uncomfortable.

### Architecture & Atmosphere
The Grid looks like a place that was simultaneously very advanced and fell apart and then was repaired by people who were very good at some things and completely indifferent to others. Cables run everywhere — along walls, across streets, through windows. Server towers occupy floors of buildings whose facades are blackened and broken. Cooling systems protrude from walls at odd angles. The streets are lit with an even, cold blue-white light from high-efficiency LEDs, and that light runs day and night because night and day don't mean much to the people who work here.

The upper floors of the main cluster are dense with screens — windows have been covered and replaced with displays showing data feeds, maps, communications, and art that blurs the boundary between data visualization and aesthetic intent. Flying over The Grid at night, it would look like a cluster of glowing coals.

### Key Locations

**The Node** — The central server complex from which The Grid's network is administered. The Node is a large, purpose-modified building that is essentially one continuous technical system, running on dedicated power, maintained by a rotating team of engineers who live and work on-site in small, spartan apartments. The Node is guarded less by weapons than by layers of electronic security and the simple fact that breaking in physically would require destroying the thing you came for. The Node's lead administrator is a figure called **The Weave** — a title held by whoever currently runs the network's core functions. The current Weave is a young woman named **Petra Null**, twenty-six years old, who has held the position for three years and shows no sign of giving it up.

**The Open Exchange** — A large marketplace in the western blocks of the district where information — and information-related services — are openly bought and sold. Surveillance records. Communications interception. Data recovery from pre-Darkening systems. Research into archived records. Identity construction or destruction. The Exchange operates on a strict protocol of **Verified Anonymity** — you can transact without revealing who you are, but your transactions are recorded and can be retrieved by Grid authority if a sufficiently serious dispute arises. This system, counterintuitively, creates significant trust.

**The Blindspot** — Every network has holes, and The Grid's network has one deliberate one: a section of three blocks in the eastern district that is genuinely, carefully shielded from the network. No cameras. No sensors. No recorded communications. The Blindspot is where Grid residents and the people they trust go when they don't want to be in the system. What happens in the Blindspot is, by Grid convention, unknowable. By practical reality, it is the location of The Grid's most sensitive and most ambivalent activities.

**The Ghost Archive** — A collection of recovered pre-Darkening data that has been at least partially reconstructed by Grid archivists over decades. The Ghost Archive contains fragments of the old internet — social media posts, news archives, entertainment, scientific research, corporate communications. Access is tiered and expensive. Some sections are restricted without clear explanation. Researchers who have tried to access the most restricted sections have been politely redirected. Those who have persisted have not been seen in The Grid afterward — though they've been confirmed alive in other districts, apparently of their own choice.

**The Antenna Forest** — The rooftops of the northern Grid blocks are covered in communication equipment — antennas, dishes, and devices of less obvious purpose pointing in multiple directions, including upward. The Grid maintains that this is the remains of old broadcast infrastructure repurposed for city-wide communication. The question of what — if anything — the Antenna Forest might be trying to contact, or receive from, in directions that are neither "toward the city" nor "toward the outer zones," is not one that Grid officials encourage.

### Atmosphere for Play
The Grid is the city's information layer made physical — the place where the question "who knows what?" becomes concrete and immediate. It is a district of secrets managed, of surveillance traded as currency, of knowledge as power in its most direct form. The stories here involve the archaeology of the pre-Darkening world, the ethics of information, the question of what certain data could do if it reached certain people, and the creeping possibility that the network — seventy years running without a true reset — might have developed characteristics that nobody programmed.

### Story Seeds
- A Grid data-runner has recovered a fragment from the Ghost Archive that appears to show pre-Darkening communications about Mycorvax-7 — communications between parties that should not have been in contact with each other. She's trying to decide what it's worth and whether she'll survive long enough to collect.
- Someone has been accessing the Blindspot using a physical key that should not exist — it predates the current administration and several administrations before it. What they're doing in the Blindspot is unknown. That it has happened at all is terrifying.
- The Antenna Forest has received something. The Grid is not discussing what. Three different parties have already come to offer extraordinary sums for whatever it is — and they arrived before any public announcement.

## DISTRICT SIX: THE CLINIC
*"We keep you alive. What you do with that is your problem."*

### Overview
The Clinic is not, technically, a single medical facility — though it contains several significant ones. It's a district that grew up around the concentration of medical knowledge, practice, and resource that formed in the years immediately after the Darkening, when the surviving doctors, nurses, pharmacologists, and medical engineers clustered together out of pure practical necessity. Over seventy years, this clustering has calcified into something like a culture — a district whose identity is built around medicine, biological research, and the particular kind of wisdom and grimness that comes from working at the edge of human survival for three generations.

**15,000 to 20,000 people** live in The Clinic. It is located in the southern-central city, between The Shambles to the north and the outer perimeter wall to the south.

### Population & Demographics
Medical professionals form the core of Clinic culture, but around them has grown a broader community of people who came for treatment and stayed, or who were born here, or who found that proximity to medicine was the best survival strategy in a world where disease is a genuine existential threat. There's a significant research population — scientists who dedicate their lives to understanding Mycorvax-7, developing new treatments, and investigating the biology of the Touched.

The district has also become home to a substantial population of people with severe disabilities or chronic illnesses — people who need medical proximity to survive. This gives The Clinic a particular demographic texture that distinguishes it from every other district: here, bodies in all their variations are simply normal facts of life, and the adjustment required of outsiders who carry unconscious assumptions about ability and health is real and occasionally uncomfortable.

### Architecture & Atmosphere
The Clinic is cleaner than most of the city — not pristine, but genuinely maintained. Streets are kept clear, waste is managed carefully, and there's a culture of collective hygiene that the district enforces through social pressure and, where necessary, through the significant practical power that comes from being the people who decide who receives care.

The major medical facilities are large, well-lit, and staffed with exhausted, competent professionals who have learned to function at the edge of their resources. The residential areas around them range from the relatively comfortable quarters of senior medical staff to the crowded dormitory spaces where patient families camp while waiting, sometimes for months.

The architecture mixes old hospital structures with repurposed commercial buildings and new construction in roughly equal measure, giving the district a functional patchwork look that is somehow less depressing than it should be, possibly because everything that's built here is built to last.

### Key Locations

**Central Medical Complex** — Three interconnected hospital buildings that form the largest healthcare facility in Necropolis Nova. The CMC handles everything from routine care to surgery to the treatment of Mycorvax-7 exposure cases. It runs on a triage system of brutal efficiency and a payment structure of even more brutal flexibility — they will take anything of value in exchange for care, including labor, information, and in documented cases, oaths of service. The CMC's Director is **Dr. Emre Valen**, a fifty-eight year old surgeon who has been running the CMC for twenty years and who everyone agrees is the best doctor in the city and one of the most politically calculating people alive.

**The Spore Research Institute** — The closest thing to a formal scientific research facility in Necropolis Nova. The Institute is dedicated to the study of Mycorvax-7, the Blighted, and the Touched — in that order of official priority, and roughly the reverse order of secret priority. The Institute's published findings are the most authoritative scientific voice in the city. Its unpublished findings are among the most dangerous secrets in Necropolis Nova.

**The Hospice Quarter** — The eastern section of The Clinic has been largely given over to end-of-life care. The Hospice Quarter has developed its own culture over seventy years — less grim than outsiders expect, more focused on the management of meaning than the management of pain. There are gardens here, and musicians, and people who have made it their life's work to help other people through the last part of theirs.

**The Black Lab** — Not officially acknowledged, The Black Lab is known to exist by most of the city's sophisticated operators as a private research facility operating somewhere in the sub-basement levels of the western Clinic blocks. It conducts medical experiments that the Institute cannot officially sanction. It produces treatments that the CMC cannot officially administer. It is tolerated because it works and occasionally produces results that save lives that nothing else could have saved. The people who run it believe that this justifies everything. The people who have ended up as subjects of its experiments would disagree, if they were in a position to do so.

**The Garden of Remembrance** — An outdoor space on the Clinic's roof terraces, carefully maintained, where the names of patients who have died over seventy years of operation are recorded on long metal panels. The Garden of Remembrance is also, practically, a place where people who want to have conversations that are not taking place in a building can have them — and The Clinic's location relative to the political center of the city means that some important conversations have happened here, among the long lists of names.

### Atmosphere for Play
The Clinic is the city's conscience in physical form — the place where the cost of everything that happens everywhere else becomes undeniable. The stories here are about human limits, about what knowledge costs, about the difference between care and control, and about the slow, terrible work of understanding a catastrophe that has already happened. The Touched are studied here and sometimes helped here and sometimes used here, which creates a moral texture that rewards play.

### Story Seeds
- A new Mycorvax-7 variant has been identified in three patients — one from The Shambles, one from The Forge, and one from outside The Perimeter who was brought in by a Scrapper team. Dr. Valen is keeping it quiet while the Institute investigates. The Black Lab is running its own investigation, for reasons it hasn't shared.
- An elderly patient in the Hospice Quarter has asked to speak to someone she describes as "not from the medical establishment, not from any faction, just someone who will listen." She says she knows something about the Darkening — something she witnessed directly, seventy years ago — that she has never told anyone. She says she is running out of time to be careful about who knows.
- Research records from the Spore Research Institute have been accessed without authorization — not stolen, just *read*. Whoever accessed them looked at exactly one file, and that file concerns a specific pattern of ability development in Touched individuals that the Institute had classified at the highest level.
